ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The picture uses small towers to illustrate the process of moving bricks. The upper-left picture shows that the top two bricks of the old tower are 50 on top and 49 below; the lower-right picture shows that a pair taken down later in the new tower, with 48 on top and 47 below, is placed on top of the pair taken down earlier, with 50 on top and 49 below. The picture also shows that the internal top-bottom order of each pair of bricks remains unchanged, for example 2 is still above 1, and 4 is still above 3. Reasoning: The original tower is numbered from 1 to 50 from bottom to top, so the two bricks taken down each time from the top of the old tower are, in order, (50,49), (48,47), (46,45), …, (2,1), where each pair of parentheses indicates that the upper brick comes first. When each pair is placed on the top of the new tower, its internal order remains unchanged, but the whole pair taken down later will press on top of the whole pair taken down earlier, so finally the new tower from top to bottom is (2,1), (4,3), (6,5), …, (50,49). In the relevant part, the final order contains …, (26,25), (28,27), (30,29), …, so 27 is the lower brick of the pair (28,27), while the next pair (30,29) is below it, so 27 is exactly above 30.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram first: it shows brick 50 above 49 as the first top pair removed from the old tower, and the new tower example has later removed pairs, such as 48 above 47, placed on top of the earlier pair 50 above 49. Thus each two-brick block keeps its internal top-to-bottom order, but the blocks themselves are stacked in reverse removal order. From the text, the original tower is numbered 1 at the bottom up to 50 at the top. So the removed ordered pairs are (50,49), (48,47), ..., (2,1), and the final tower from top to bottom is (2,1), (4,3), (6,5), ..., (50,49). In this list, around the relevant labels we have ..., (26,25), (28,27), (30,29), ...; therefore brick 27 is directly above brick 30.
